header.title: Commonitorium De Coelestio Imperatori Oblatum: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Marius Mercator
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tmp772.tmp772.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. The whole work is translated. It was chosen because no English translation of it could be found.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation of the whole work, checked against the original by a second AI only in samples. No specialist has reviewed it.
header.availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

Evident scanning errors and stray footnote letters have been silently corrected. Marginal variants from Baluze's edition ([Bal. ...]) have been left out of the English, except at 2.5, where the bracketed words are needed to complete the sentence; the stray 'Est' after them is not translated.

Head, 2: 'in praesenti' is unclear; it may mean 'in person' rather than 'at the present time'.

1.1a: the letters before 'memoriae Ambrosii' are illegible; 'of holy memory' is a conjecture from the formula used elsewhere in this text.

1.2a: 'ad sum Asiae Romani episcopi' is corrupt; 'Asiae' seems intruded and a word or name may be lost. Translated as 'to the examination of the bishop of Rome'.

1.5a: 'pra-Vi(??)cre' is corrupt and the word could not be established with confidence (possibly 'praeclare', 'clearly'); it is marked [...].

2.3: 'Cum sic, inquit qui peccant similiter et moriuntur' seems faulty; translated by its evident sense.

2.4: the sentence 'sive in eos ... sed in eos' is awkward; Baluze's 'et' would give 'but also over those who...'. 'Animam' follows the biblical sense of life in the blood.

2.10: 'quam nobis liberatos donavit' is ungrammatical as printed; translated as if 'qua nos liberatos donavit'. 3.1a: Zosimus's letter is known as the Tractoria; the word is kept in italics. 3.4: the end of the verb is damaged in the scan ('de(??)r-sisse'), probably 'delusisse' (deceived) or 'derisisse' (mocked); 'deceived' is a conjecture. 3.5: 'Theodolus' read as Theodotus, as elsewhere in this passage; 'lociu' read as 'locis'. 4.3: 'libellus' here means a booklet, not the 'written complaint' of the glossary; so also in 4.6. 'Livaniam' is Mercator's name for the widow addressed; the form is kept as printed. 'implerent' read as a singular ('impleverit' or similar), required by 'simplex ille est'. 4.4: 'Coelestinus' read as Coelestius; 'quod legem Evangelium appellat' is literally 'calls the law the Gospel', but the sense of the argument requires that he is not wrong to call the Gospel a law, and it is so rendered; the scan has a lost sign at 'sub (??) simili'. 4.5: the quoted verse 'Christ has redeemed us' is Gal. 3:13; the edition's reference gives 3:10, the source of the inner quotation. 'quod si ita, quod absit, tamen ut ille vult sit dictum' is awkward and the rendering is tentative. 5.1a: 'non recte sentire' with 'confidunt' is rendered literally; the sense is presumably 'whom they are confident do not think rightly'.

From 'Admonitio' onward the text is not Mercator's but the prefatory note of his modern editor, who speaks of 'we' and cites Mercator; the italics of the printed quotations are not preserved here, and the bracketed citations are the editor's. Scanning errors silently corrected include quoestio/quaestio, Adoe/Adae, bumani/humani, iu/in and arvi/aevi; 'partei' is read as 'parte I'. 'Bassula' is the deacon usually called Bessula, the Carthaginian representative at Ephesus. Pientius is not identified in this passage. 'Unfinished Work' renders Opus Imperfectum, Augustine's last reply to Julian.

nodes.text: THE MEMORANDUM OF MARIUS MERCATOR CONCERNING CAELESTIUS, PRESENTED TO THE EMPEROR,
Whose title in the ancient copies is:

Copy of the Memorandum concerning Caelestius, which was submitted in the Greek language by Mercator not only to the Church of Constantinople but also to very many most religious men; it was also presented to the most pious prince Theodosius, ever Augustus; the same [document] was translated from Greek into Latin by the same Marius Mercator, servant of Christ, in the consulship of Florentius and Dionysius, men of senatorial rank. Through this Memorandum, once the most deadly error had become known, by imperial command both Julian, its defender and follower, with the rest of his associates and partners, and afterwards Caelestius himself, were thrust out of the city of Constantinople; and at the synod of Ephesus too they were afterwards condemned by the sentence of two hundred and seventy-five bishops in the present [time].
CHAPTER ONE.
On the case of Caelestius, how it was conducted at Carthage, Constantinople and Rome.

1. A certain Caelestius, a eunuch from his mother's womb, a disciple and hearer of Pelagius, left the city of Rome some twenty years ago, more or less, and came to Carthage, the metropolis of all Africa. There, in the presence of Aurelius, bishop of the said city, he was accused on the charges written below in a written complaint by a certain Paulinus, a deacon of Ambrose of holy memory, bishop of Milan, as the record of the proceedings shows, into which that same complaint is inserted (we have copies of these proceedings in our hands). [It was alleged] that he not only taught this himself, but had also sent through the provinces various persons in league with him, to spread these things among the peoples, namely:
That Adam was made mortal, and would have died whether he sinned or did not sin.
That Adam's sin harmed him alone, and not the human race.
That infants who are born are in the state in which Adam was before the transgression.
That the whole human race neither dies through the death or transgression of Adam, nor does the whole human race rise again through the resurrection of Christ.
That the Law sends [people] to the kingdom of heaven in the same way as the Gospel does.
That even before the coming of the Lord there were sinless human beings, that is, without sin.

2. On all these charges, as is clear from the above-mentioned copies of the synodal proceedings, the Fathers and bishops of that region opposed Caelestius and ordered him to condemn these same things, because they were of heretical meaning. But Caelestius, in no way acquiescing, and indeed resisting in those same proceedings, was deprived of ecclesiastical communion. From this sentence he thought he should appeal to the examination of the bishop of Rome; but he soon disregarded this appeal and hurried to Ephesus, a city of Asia, and there dared to seek by stealth a place in the presbyterate.

3. From there, some years later, under Atticus, bishop of holy memory, he made for the city of Constantinople, where, being detected in similar [teachings], he was thrust out of the aforesaid gracious city through the great zeal of that holy man, and letters concerning him were sent to the bishops in Asia, at Thessalonica and at Carthage; we have copies of these and are ready to produce them.

4. Yet the aforesaid Caelestius, thrown out from here as well, proceeded in all haste to the city of Rome under Zosimus, bishop of holy memory. There he was questioned in proceedings (of which we have copies), and when he was somewhat alarmed by that judge, he sowed hope in advance through his frequent replies and statements, promising that he would condemn those charges on which he had been accused at Carthage. For this was what he was being pressingly ordered to do, and for this very reason he was deemed worthy of some kindness from that holy priest; and so he obtained a certain letter, full of benevolence, to the African bishops, which he has abused, and still abuses, to deceive many who are ignorant.

5. But when the bishops wrote back from Africa and set out the whole case that had been conducted before them, and also sent from there the proceedings that had then been drawn up with him or concerning him, he was summoned to a fuller hearing, so that he might hasten to fulfil what he had promised, that is, that once the aforesaid charges had been condemned, he might be released from the sentence of the African bishops by which he had been deprived of communion. Not only did he fail to appear, but he even fled from the said city of Rome, and for this reason he was utterly condemned by the aforesaid Zosimus, bishop of blessed memory, in very full and very lengthy writings, in which are contained both the very charges on which he had been accused, and the whole case, concerning both the above-mentioned Caelestius and Pelagius his master, which seems to be [...] narrated. We too have copies of these writings here, and we submit that similar and identical writings were sent to the bishops of the Eastern Churches, the diocese of Egypt, Constantinople, Thessalonica and Jerusalem.
CHAPTER II.
On the teaching of Pelagius, of what kind it is known to be from his own writings.

1. Now the reason why Pelagius too was condemned together with him is this. Before the devastation of the city of Rome, the said man dared to compose commentaries on the apostle Paul, and to publish them for those on whose friendship he presumed; and he thought he was explaining each of the Apostle's words and meanings. So in the Epistle to the Romans, when he had come to those places where the vessel of election speaks thus: "Therefore, just as through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin death, and so death passed through to all human beings" (Rom. 5:12), he believed they should be expounded in this way. We have this book of his, and we produce it to refute his hostile error.

2. Thus, then, he says: "'Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death': He used, he says, an example or image, because just as, when there was no sin, it came in stealthily through Adam, so too, when righteousness had not remained with anyone, life was restored through Christ."

3. "'And death passed through to all human beings': Since, he says, those who sin in this way also die likewise; for death did not pass through either to Abraham, or to Isaac, or to Jacob, of whom the Lord says: 'To him all live' (Luke 20:38). Here, however, he says, he says that all are dead for this reason: because, in the multitude of sinners, the few righteous are not excepted, just as he also says there: 'There is no one who does good, there is not even one' (Ps. 52:2, 4). And again that other saying, he says: 'Every man is a liar' (Ps. 115:11); or at any rate it passed through to all those who have lived in human fashion, not heavenly."

4. And shortly afterwards: "'But death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who did not transgress in the likeness of Adam's transgression' (Rom. 5:14): Either, he says, when there was no one to distinguish between the righteous and the unrighteous, death thought it was lord over all; or over those who, like Adam, transgressed a commandment, that is, of the sons of Noah, who were commanded not to eat life in blood, and of the sons of Abraham, to whom circumcision was commanded; but over those who, apart from the commandment, had despised the natural law."

5. "'Who is a type of the one to come' (ibid.): Because, he says, just as Adam was formed by God without intercourse, so Christ too came forth from a Virgin, by the Holy Spirit's fashioning; or, as some say, a type by contrast, that is, [as the one was the head of sin, so also this one is the head of righteousness]."
6. "'But not as the offence, so also the gift' (ibid. 15): Lest, he says, equality should be supposed in the type."

7. "'For if by the transgression of one many died, much more has the gift and grace of God abounded to many through one man, Christ' (ibid.). Grace, says the Apostle, he says, had more power in giving life than sin in killing, because Adam killed not only himself but also his posterity, whereas Christ set free both those who were then in the body and those who were to come afterwards."

8. Here let the careful Catholic reader note what he says: "Adam harmed not only himself but also his posterity." Keep in mind his earlier definition: for he says here that not all human beings everywhere and altogether were harmed by that man's sin, but only those who by imitation, likewise, through their own sins and deeds, became guilty of transgression, as Adam did; and these, without doubt, are found to be those very descendants and posterity of his.

9. "But those, he says, who hold views against the transmission of sin try to attack sharply those who defend the transmission: If, they say, the sin of Adam harmed even those who do not sin, then the righteousness of Christ also benefits those who do not believe; since the Apostle says that in like manner, indeed even more, [people] are set free through one than had previously perished through one. Then they say: If baptism cleanses that ancient and long-standing sin, those who are born of two baptized persons ought to be without this sin; for they will not be able to pass on to their posterity what they themselves did not have at all. To this they add: Since, if the soul does not come by transmission, as indeed it does not, but only the flesh has the transmission of sin, it alone also deserves the punishment; for it is unjust that a soul born today, not from the mass of Adam, should bear so ancient a sin belonging to another; moreover, it is reasonable that God, who forgives [a person's] own sins, should not impute another's."

10. And again in another discourse of his the same Pelagius says: "If a sinner, he says, has begotten a sinner, so that the original sin of his little child is loosed in the receiving of baptism, then a righteous man ought to have begotten a righteous one. If, he says, their own sins do not harm parents after their conversion, much less will they be able to harm their children through them. If it befell the first man to be the cause of death, then through Christ's coming it was no longer necessary to die. If death had arisen through the sin of Adam, we would never die after the forgiveness of sins, by which he granted us to be set free. Thus the sin of Adam had more power in killing absolutely all human beings than the grace of Christ in saving, which has benefited not all, but only those who believe; for not all who are born from Adam are also reborn in Christ." And so on.
CHAPTER III.
On the condemnation of Pelagius and Caelestius, and especially of Pelagius, both by the Roman pontiffs Innocent and Zosimus and by the Fathers of Diospolis and Theodotus, bishop of Antioch.

1. All the charges written above, as has already been said earlier, are contained in that letter of Bishop Zosimus of blessed memory which is called the *Tractoria* [circular letter], by which Caelestius and Pelagius were condemned; and which, sent both to Constantinople and throughout the whole world, was confirmed by the signatures of the holy Fathers. Julian and his other accomplices, refusing to sign it and unwilling to make themselves of one mind with those same Fathers, were deposed and removed from office not only by imperial laws but also by priestly decrees, and were driven out of all Italy. Of these very many came to their senses and, corrected from the aforesaid error, returned as suppliants to the apostolic see, and on being received they recovered their churches.

2. The aforesaid Caelestius and Pelagius, indeed, were evidently not then condemned for the first time by Zosimus of holy memory, but by his predecessor Innocent of holy remembrance, by whom Julian too had been ordained. And since [Julian], after their condemnation and up to the departure of the aforesaid Innocent from this life, remained in his communion, persevering in the sincere judgement and in communion with the one who condemned the aforesaid men, he too without doubt condemned Pelagius and Caelestius; and what he now wants, or what he complains about, we do not know.

3. Now the cause of their being condemned by Innocent of holy remembrance was this. After the devastation of the city of Rome, Pelagius was living in Palestine. Certain zealous bishops found books of his, in which many and various things are seen to have been written against the Catholic faith. These were sent with letters to the Fathers and bishops in Africa, where, three councils having been assembled, the said books were read. Then, when reports were sent from there to Rome and the books themselves were dispatched along with them, the apostolic verdict went forth from [Innocent] as he wrote back to the aforesaid councils, which deprived those same men, Caelestius and Pelagius, of ecclesiastical communion; and we have copies of these writings in our hands.

4. While still residing at Jerusalem, Pelagius was also accused before a synod, and at first indeed, by evasion, covering himself with certain ambiguous professions and setting out or answering doubtful statements, he seems at that time to have deceived the hearing of the bishops.

5. But afterwards, clearly caught out at the insistence of his accusers and exposed by a later synod, over which Theodotus of holy memory, bishop of Antioch, presided, he was also driven out of the holy and venerable places of Jerusalem. This is attested by the letters of the same holy Theodotus and of Praylius of holy remembrance, bishop of Jerusalem, sent to the most reverend bishop of the city of Rome, copies of which we have in our hands as evidence.
CHAPTER IV.
On the shared opinion and condemnation of both heretics.

1. Now in the very accusation of the charges that were then brought against this same Pelagius, this also was included, along with other execrable things that his disciple Caelestius held, namely: "Infants, even if they are not baptized, have eternal life."

2. That charge too which was set down above, which we mentioned was held by Caelestius and was in agreement with the teaching of his master, namely, "The Law sends [people] to the kingdom of heaven just as the Gospel does," Pelagius openly confirms and declares in certain of his writings.

3. Indeed there is a booklet of his, which we have in our hands, addressed to a certain widow Livania, containing a discourse of exhortation, in which it is said thus: "It befits a handmaid of Christ, he says, to pursue simplicity: not that which is folly rather than simplicity, but that of which [Scripture] has written: 'Blessed is every simple soul' (Proverbs 11:27, according to the Septuagint); while Scripture says elsewhere: 'Cursed is every man who does not abide in all the things that are written in the book of the law, so as to do them' (Deut. 27:26). From this, he says, it is shown that true simplicity is not that which despises God's commandments with senseless complacency, but that which keeps the precepts of the law with wise fear; for in saying that he is cursed who does not abide in the things that are written, [Scripture] by contrast means that he who has not kept all the precepts is not blessed. And if every simple person is blessed, then the simple person is the one who fulfils all the precepts of the law."

4. That he asserts what has so often been said above, "The books of Moses send [people] to the kingdom of heaven just as the Gospel does," no Catholic who has read this charge doubts, nor will he be able to meet any difficulty in understanding it. And since he named the law without distinction in this same most impious charge: if [he means] the Mosaic [law], whose testimony of the curse he has cited, he openly tries to draw us into Judaism; but if, to cover himself by deceit, he should say that by the name of law he meant the Gospel, then in calling the Gospel a law he does not indeed err. But he is impious in this, that he does not shrink from placing us, who are under the Gospel, under a similar and equal curse, making the grace of the Gospel equal to the law of circumcision and to all Judaism. Hence also his disciple Caelestius dared openly to declare: "The Law sends [people] to the kingdoms of heaven just as the Gospel does."

5. For it is clear, according to Pelagius, that if we are still under the same or a similar bond, even in the time of the Gospel, then if we have erred in anything, as human beings do, or have not fulfilled one of the precepts of the Gospel, we are cursed. But if it has been said thus, which God forbid, in the way he wants, the Gospel has been made equal to the old law; and where then will be the saying of the Apostle Paul: 'Christ has redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us, because it is written (Deut. 27:26): Cursed is every man who does not abide in all the things that are written in the book of the law, so as to do them' (Gal. 3:10)?

6. Moreover, going further on, he develops this same thought more broadly in the same discourse of this booklet, and commends it more broadly. For after many things he says in the same place: "To hate, to curse and to envy, to lie, to disparage and to believe those who disparage, is thought to be a slight sin or none at all; but those who think this have forgotten that we read that those liable [for breaking] even a slight commandment are to be handed over to Gehenna. For it is clear, he says, that the Lord said: Whoever says to his brother, 'Fool' or 'Raca,' will be liable to Gehenna."
CHAPTER V.
Julian is addressed and invited to come to his senses by the example of his associates.

1. Let Julian, then, and the others who share with him, at least now condemn these men caught in such most impious errors, namely Pelagius and Caelestius, for the satisfaction of the Church; and if there are any whom they trust do not think rightly against the Catholic faith, let them not hesitate to point them out by name, and in ecclesiastical order they will receive a reply from us as far as we are able, or at any rate from the one whom they say deviates from the Catholic sense.

2. For as we said above, many who had followed Caelestius and Pelagius with him, and had also become sharers and associates of Julian, have now abandoned him and, Pelagius having been condemned, submitting themselves to the apostolic see and professing repentance for what they had wrongly thought, were held worthy of mercy by the holy Fathers and were received.
PREFATORY NOTE ON THE FOLLOWING BOOK OF SUBNOTATIONS BY MARIUS MERCATOR.

This work was divided by Mercator into two parts. One received the name of Memorandum to the reader, because it stands in place of a preface; the other, that of Subnotations on the words of Julian, which is the Work proper. Both contain many quite outstanding things; but the first chiefly those that concern history; the second, those that concern doctrine, although it too reveals certain things about Julian unknown to this very day.

One question is proposed here to be treated in its own right, concerning the mortality of Adam through sin: others are touched on as appendices, concerning original sin, concerning the baptism and redemption of little children, etc. Hence Mercator (In the Memorandum or Prologue of this book, part I): The whole sum of the inept and still more impious labour of Julian seems to be reduced to one depraved opinion, namely that the transgression of Adam and Eve did not make them mortal. And afterwards (At the end of the book of Subnotations): You know that your whole case is built entirely on this question that is being debated between us, concerning the mortality, that is, of the human race, which through the first transgressors of the divine command has run generally through the seeds, and runs, and will run to the very end.

As to the date, I think something can probably be gathered from this. Mercator wrote after the death of Theodore of Mopsuestia, as is clear from these words (At the beginning of the Prologue or Memorandum): By Theodore, formerly bishop of the town of Mopsuestia; indeed after the death of St Augustine: Augustine, the bishop of holy memory, at various times, etc.; and also after the publication of his reply to Julian's last work. For Mercator says thus (Ibid., towards the end): St Augustine in his six books overturned his first four, and also the later eight, by his replies set beneath each chapter: and when the Work of both came into our hands, etc.

Since, then, Theodore departed this life in the year 427, and Augustine in the year 430 (Theodoret at the end of the Ecclesiastical History), and the Unfinished Work could scarcely have reached Mercator, who was in the East, before the deacon Bassula came to Ephesus, who, as is credible, brought this Work together with the letter of Capreolus, bishop of Carthage, as the sacred testament of a most holy man dying in defence of grace; it does not seem far from the truth that the Subnotations were indeed made by Mercator towards the end of the year 431, in which the synod was held at Ephesus, but were collected into one book at the urging of Pientius in the following year; for without doubt what usually happens to the curious will have happened to Mercator: he will have read eagerly a Work long awaited as soon as he received it, annotated it once read, and in due time gathered the Subnotations into one.

It is in the reader's interest to have observed three things here. First, that we have indeed divided the Subnotations into eight chapters, but have followed Mercator in this, who set before himself that number of excerpts from the books of Julian for examination; and that we have marked off each chapter, and the Memorandum itself, with various numbers, so that if anything must at some time be cited by us, it may be found the more easily the more indications it is marked with. Second, that to each excerpt of Julian the reply of Augustine, although Mercator did not add it, has nevertheless been appended by us, so that the replies of the two doctors, set beside each other, may shed light on one another. Last, that nowhere, whether in Mercator or in other authors of the same age, are more secrets contained in themselves that pertain to the history of the Caelestians, so that someone might deservedly for that reason call this little work: The Mystery of the Caelestian Heresy Revealed.
